title: Paloma and the Harbor
premise: Paloma Reyes has spent ten years writing anonymous letters to the family her testimony once destroyed, hiding in a coastal town where nobody asks questions. When Dominic Lockridge inherits the neighboring vineyard—buried under debts left by his late father, the very man Paloma's letters were addressed to—the two are drawn together by a shared drought and a leaking harbor wall. As their reluctant alliance deepens into love, Paloma must decide whether to confess that she was the witness whose words sent his father to prison, while Dominic uncovers evidence his father was framed by the vineyard's creditors. In the end, Paloma chooses truth over invisibility: she testifies again, this time to clear a dead man's name, and Dominic chooses her anyway, proving that second chances arrive exactly when they're needed.
about_author: Marguerite Sterling is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent years cataloguing letters found in coastal lighthouses. She writes romances about people who believe they've run out of time, from a cottage overlooking the same fog-bound harbor that haunts her fiction.

chapters.title: The Last Train
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She mails her tenth anonymous letter on the anniversary of the trial, then learns the Lockridge heir is moving into the derelict vineyard next door. Panic and routine war within her; the emotional beat is the fragile illusion of safety cracking for the first time.

chapters.title: Debts Instead of Grapes
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. He surveys the dying vines and crushing liabilities his father left behind, meeting Paloma when she returns a stray dog that wandered through the fence line. Wary courtesy between neighbors; the beat is two guarded people recognizing exhaustion in each other.

chapters.title: What the Harbor Keeps
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. A storm breaches the old seawall separating both properties, forcing them into an emergency repair effort with the town's few remaining hands. Working side by side, Dominic mentions his father's imprisonment; Paloma nearly confesses. The beat is intimacy born of shared labor and shared secrets.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Tuesdays
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Sorting his father's study, he finds every one of Paloma's unsigned letters, kept in a shoebox labeled 'Tuesdays.' He becomes obsessed with identifying the writer even as he falls for the woman next door. The beat is tenderness tangled with suspicion.

chapters.title: Salt and Confession
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. At the harbor festival, Dominic tells her the letters 'kept my father alive' in prison, and she almost tells him everything—but a creditor's lawyer appears, threatening foreclosure. The beat is hope deferred; she chooses silence again and hates herself for it.

chapters.title: The Creditor's Ledger
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Digging through loan documents to fight foreclosure, he discovers discrepancies suggesting his father discovered embezzlement by the vineyard's investors before his conviction. The beat is grief inverted—his father may have been guilty of honesty, not fraud.

chapters.title: Ink Under Her Fingernails
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Dominic confronts her gently with a letter and her handwriting on a borrowed notepad. She confesses: at nineteen, coerced by the investors' lawyer, she gave false testimony that sealed his father's fate. The beat is devastation—love offered and seemingly lost in the same breath.

chapters.title: After the Last Train Leaves
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Furious and hollowed out, he nearly puts Paloma on the evening train out of town, but the creditor's men arrive to seize the property that night. Standing in the vineyard rows, he realizes the woman who lied to save herself at nineteen is the only person now willing to risk everything to make it right. The beat is the choice to let someone stay.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Climax. She files to reopen the case, testifying publicly against the investors who coerced her, while Dominic presents the ledger as corroborating evidence. The courtroom scene strips away her decade of hiding; the beat is terror transfigured into courage as justice finally moves outside and inside the law.

chapters.title: First Harvest
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Months later, the conviction is posthumously overturned, the creditors are indicted, and the vineyard—saved by a community grant—yields its first real harvest. Dominic and Paloma press grapes together where the seawall once stood repaired. The beat is quiet joy: survival was the price, but love is what it bought.
